hook: The bookbinder's boy who discovered how to make electricity from magnetism.

pages.x: Michael Faraday was born in 1791 in south London, the son of a poor blacksmith. He had little schooling. At 14 he was apprenticed to a bookbinder, and read the books he bound, above all the ones about electricity and chemistry.

pages.t: The notes that got him a job
pages.x: In 1812 a customer gave him tickets to hear the famous chemist Humphry Davy lecture. Faraday wrote up careful notes, bound them into a book and sent them to Davy, asking for work. When Davy's assistant was sacked for fighting, Faraday got the job.
In 1821 he made a wire carrying an electric current spin round and round a magnet. It was the first electric motor.
pages.fx: Every electric motor, from fans and washing machines to trains and electric cars, works on the same idea.

pages.x: In 1831 he found that moving a magnet in and out of a coil of wire makes an electric current flow. He built the first generator, a copper disc spinning between the poles of a magnet.
pages.fx: Almost all the world's electricity is still made this way, in generators turned by steam, water or wind.

pages.x: In 1825 he started the Christmas Lectures at the Royal Institution, science shows for young people. His talk on the chemistry of a candle is still in print, and the lectures still run on television every year.

A famous story says a politician asked him what use electricity was. "Why, sir," Faraday replied, "there is every probability that you will soon be able to tax it." The story is probably made up, but it was right.

He turned down a knighthood, and twice refused to lead the Royal Society, wanting to stay "plain Mr Faraday to the end". He also refused to help the government make poison gas for the Crimean War. He died in 1867.
Faraday made the age of electricity possible: motors, generators and transformers all come from his work. Einstein kept a picture of him on his study wall.
pts: Discovered how to make electricity from magnetism
Started the Christmas Lectures for young people
